sections.html:
Laredo owners usually weigh an as-is cash sale against a regular listing. The better fit depends on how much work the house needs and how soon you need the money. Laredo is a border city on the Rio Grande, in southwestern Webb County, and many buyers have jobs tied to freight, customs and logistics. Older homes cluster near downtown and newer subdivisions spread outward, so a house's age points to the building codes it was built under.

An investor who pays cash generally accepts the property in its present state, so you skip permit fees and contractor bids. A listing can attract more bidders but adds repairs, showings and the wait on a buyer's lender. Run both numbers against your own deadline before you sign anything.

A short list of questions comes up before most Laredo offers. Answers in hand speed up any sale.

  • Does the house sit in the floodplain? The city handles that through a separate floodplain development permit.
  • Were past additions, porches, carports or block fences built with permits?
  • How old is the roof, and was electrical, plumbing and cooling work done by registered trade contractors?
  • Is the property tax bill current, and which exemptions are on file?

Unpermitted work will not block a cash sale, but an informed buyer will lower the price for it.

sections.h2: Do Laredo permits matter when selling?
sections.html:
They can. The city requires a building permit for remodels, additions, porches, carports, block fences and demolitions. Building Development Services follows the International Residential Code and allows up to 21 days for residential review.

Electrical, mechanical, plumbing, irrigation and mobile home installation permits have to be pulled by a contractor in that trade. A homeowner may pull a general permit but is treated as the contractor on the job. When records are missing, the city offers an Amnesty Certificate of Occupancy, which requires proof that the structure has been occupied continuously since August 2, 1983.

Sample residential permit fees from the City of Laredo
Permit typePlan check feePermit fee
Block fence$30.00$46.00
Reroof$34.00$50.00
Open accessory (porch, palapa, carport)$40.00$64.00
Remodel or addition, up to 1,000 sq. ft.$40.00$64.00

A separate $20.00 technology fee applies. Fees get updated, so ask the city for its current schedule before you budget.

sections.h2: Other city permits that come up
sections.html:
Sellers tend to forget the small permits that inspectors look for. A few touch a typical residential lot.

  • Driveway work in the right-of-way needs a $50 residential permit, pulled by a registered contractor.
  • A garage sale permit costs $15, with a limit of five per year.
  • A solar panel permit carries a non-refundable $200 fee and must be in hand before work starts.
  • A permit lapses six months after issuance if work has not begun, and all work must finish within twelve months.

General contractors register with the city for a $60 fee. Had a contractor in? Request the registration and the final inspection record, because proof of approval is something a buyer's inspector may ask to see.

Laredo adopted the 2021 International codes in 2024 and keeps separate floodplain, fence and residential setback rules. Call Building Development Services if a porch or fence went up without a permit. A cash buyer may live with it, while a buyer using a loan often will not.

The Webb County tax office mails statements every October. The lump-sum deadline is January 31, and penalty and interest start February 1. A split into two halves, due November 30 and June 30, is also available.

Pair a homestead exemption with an over-65, disability or disabled veteran exemption and you may pay in four installments, due January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. For owners without a mortgage escrow, the county runs a monthly prepayment plan through September 15. To enter a plan for delinquent taxes you need your name on the account and a homestead exemption, and interest on the plan accrues monthly up to 12 percent.

Texas attaches the tax lien to the property each January 1, so an unpaid bill follows the house to its next owner. The owner on January 1 stays liable. Ask the Webb County tax office for the exact balance early, so the closing date works around it. The balance is settled from your proceeds, and the contract spells out how buyer and seller split the current year.

sections.h2: State rules that touch a Laredo closing
sections.html:
• Homestead owners get $140,000 off from school districts, and seniors and disabled owners get another $60,000.
  • Appraisals use a valuation date of January 1.
  • County clerks record deeds, and the signature must be notarized.

Webb County's appraisal district posts its own exemption forms. A loan in default can be paid off by a sale that closes ahead of the auction date.

sections.h2: If your Laredo home is in foreclosure
sections.html: A lender owes you notice of sale at least 21 days ahead, and auctions take place on a set Tuesday each month. Selling before that Tuesday can pay the loan off and halt the auction. Ask the servicer for a written payoff, pick a buyer who can close inside the window and keep the sale paperwork moving the same week you sign.

sections.h2: Steps to sell a Laredo house fast
sections.html:
1. Round up the deed, the latest tax statement, permits and a list of known repairs.
  2. Ask the Webb County tax office what is owed so there are no surprises.
  3. Request offers from cash buyers and, if you like, a listing agent, and compare net amounts.
  4. Choose a title company and sign the deed.

Selling a house you inherited? Take an affidavit of ownership interest and the death certificate to the appraisal district so the homestead exemption can be moved.

sections.h2: Papers to request from city and county
sections.html: Before listing, ask Building Development Services whether any open permit exists on the address, and ask the Webb County tax office and appraisal district for a printout of what is owed and which exemptions are active. Put those pages next to your deed and any survey. A short, organized stack lets an investor make a firm offer instead of a cautious one.

A cash buyer does not need a lender's appraisal, so the sale avoids the gap between contract and loan approval. You also skip staging, repeated showings and most repair negotiation. What you give up is some of the price. Weigh that against the cost of fixing a roof, a fence or an unpermitted porch, plus the months you would pay the mortgage, taxes and utilities while the house waits for a buyer.

Get three things in writing before you accept: who covers title and recording charges, the closing date the buyer commits to, and any condition beyond clear title.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Laredo house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Many cash buyers take homes needing work, and the offer reflects the repairs. Two or three offers show how much condition moves the number.

faqs.q: Is a permit required before putting a Laredo home on the market?
faqs.a: No permit is needed just to sell. Permits come into play only if you plan to remodel, add a porch or carport, or build a block fence before selling. Laredo's Building Development Services can tell you which projects need one.

faqs.q: What is the Webb County tax deadline?
faqs.a: The lump-sum payment is due by January 31 each year. Statements go out in October, and a split plan divides payment between November 30 and June 30.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax when a Laredo house sells?
faqs.a: The tax lien dates from January 1, which means the unpaid year's tax travels with the property. Closing usually settles the balance, and the buyer and seller divide it as the contract says.

faqs.q: What happens if my Laredo home is in foreclosure?
faqs.a: Notice of sale has to come at least 21 days ahead, and the auction falls on a set Tuesday every month. Selling first can pay off the loan and stop the auction.
